summary: This RFC changes the registration policy for several registries in the IANA PCEP Numbers group from Standards Action to IETF Review, and it allows experimental error codes. It updates a long list of earlier PCEP RFCs to match. The goal is to make it easier to get new values assigned.

eli5.summary: A club had a rule that only a vote of every member could add a new item to its list. This loosens the rule so adding things is easier, and leaves room for experiments.

questions: what are pcep experimental error types
what is ietf review vs standards action
which pcep error types are experimental
subtitle: Makes it easier to assign new PCEP values and sets aside four error types for experiments.

tldr.problem: Several IANA registries for the Path Computation Element Protocol (PCEP) could only be changed by Standards Track or Best Current Practice RFCs, and PCEP errors had no range reserved for experiments.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC changes the listed registries from Standards Action to IETF Review, and designates PCEP Error-Types 252-255 for Experimental Use.
tldr.outcome: Any type of RFC in the IETF Stream can now request values in those registries, and experiments can return their own error codes without clashing with real allocations.

today: RFC 9756 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It updates RFC 5440 and 20 other PCEP RFCs, and the registry rules it sets are the current ones for the PCEP Numbers registry group.

sections.title: Why the Registry Rules Changed
sections.content:
IANA keeps a registry group called "Path Computation Element Protocol (PCEP) Numbers". Several RFCs from the Path Computation Element (PCE) Working Group filled it. Most of its registries already use IETF Review as the registration procedure. A few use Standards Action, so their values can be assigned only through Standards Track or Best Current Practice RFCs in the IETF Stream.

This memo changes those registries to IETF Review, which lets any type of RFC in the IETF Stream make the allocation request. It also deals with experiments: RFC 8356 designated experimental ranges for PCEP messages, objects and TLV types, but not for error codes. This document updates RFC 5440 to fill that gap.
sections.eli5: The club had two rules for adding to its lists. This document makes the strict rule a bit looser, and it saves a few empty spots for tests.

sections.title: Registries Moved to IETF Review
sections.content:
Section 2 lists, in Table 1, the registries in the PCEP Numbers group whose policy changed from Standards Action to IETF Review. Each affected registry now lists this document as an additional reference. Where the change applies only to part of a registry, the Remarks column gives the range. The one such case is the Generalized Endpoint Types registry from RFC 8779, where the range is 0-244.

The table covers registries defined by many earlier RFCs, for example RFC 8231 (such as the LSP Object Flag Field), RFC 8664 (the SR-ERO Flag Field), RFC 8697 (the ASSOCIATION Type Field) and RFC 9603 (the SRv6-ERO Flag Field). That is why the RFC updates such a long list of documents.

The RFC also says that future registries in this group should prefer IETF Review over Standards Action.
sections.eli5: Lots of pages in the club book had the strict rule. Now they all follow the easier one, and new pages are told to do the same.

sections.title: Experimental Error-Types
sections.content:
IANA has designated four PCEP Error-Type codepoints, 252-255, for Experimental Use. In the "PCEP-ERROR Object Error Types and Values" registry, Error-Types 0-251 use IETF Review, and the IETF Review procedure applies to all Error-values (0-255) for Error-Types in that range. Error-Types 252-255 use Experimental Use, and that policy applies to all Error-values (0-255) under them.

IANA also added a registry entry for Error-Type 252-255, meaning "Reserved for Experimental Use", with Error-values 0-255 reserved for Experimental Use and this RFC as the reference.

The reason is practical. Experiments often need to report experiment-specific errors. Existing error codes can often be reused, but sometimes new ones are needed, and they must not collide with existing or future allocations.
sections.eli5: Four numbers are now marked as free for tests only. If you are trying a new idea, you can use one without getting in anyone's way.

sections.title: Running and Handling Experiments
sections.content:
An experiment that wants to return experimental error codes should use one of the experimental Error-Type values. The participants should agree on which Error-Type and which Error-values to use, and the experiment describes what each pair means. The RFC says these values should not be recorded in any public (especially any IETF) documentation. If several experiments run at once on the same implementations, their sets of Error-Types and Error-values must be kept distinct.

There is no scope for experimental Error-values inside existing non-experimental Error-Types. This keeps the registry and implementations simpler. If an experiment succeeds and moves to Standards Track work, each pair needs a proper assignment from IANA, and the code change is as simple as changing the numeric values.

An implementation that gets an experimental Error-Type it does not recognise treats it like any other unknown Error-Type. It will normally close the PCEP session, but is not required to act on Error-Types and may just log the error. The same holds for an unknown Error-value inside an experimental Error-Type, which can happen through a faulty implementation, out-of-sync implementations or several experiments running at once.
sections.eli5: People testing together agree on what each test number means and keep it private. A program that sees a test number it does not know just writes it down, or may hang up.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo does not change the security considerations of any updated RFC. It points to RFC 5440 and to a work-in-progress draft on PCEPS for the security measures that apply to PCEP.

RFC 3692 asserts that experimental codepoints add no new security considerations. This RFC adds a caution: implementations that accept experimental error codepoints need to think about how they parse and process them, in case they come by accident from another experiment. They also need to consider the security aspects of the experimental extensions themselves, and RFC 6709 gives design considerations for protocol extensions.
sections.eli5: Test numbers from someone else's test could show up by mistake, so a program should handle them carefully and not just trust them.

sections.title: Why All the Registries, and Why Not Objects
sections.content:
Appendix A explains why every listed registry moved, even flag fields with few bits where space is tight. The PCE Working Group decided that Working Group Last Call and IETF Last Call should be enough to handle frivolous experiments taking over the few codepoints. It adds that the group could also create a new protocol field and registry for future use, as was done in the past (see RFC 9357).

Appendix B looks at RFC 8356, which gave experimental codepoints only to messages, objects and TLV types. Its reasoning was that an experiment could use a new experimental object or TLV instead. This RFC says that using an object to carry arbitrary experimental errors would cause unnecessary divergence in the code, and that experimental Error-Types are a better approach because they make it easier to move successful experiments onto the Standards Track.
sections.eli5: Some worried that tiny lists could fill up with silly tests. The group decided that review steps would catch that, and that real test numbers are better than clumsy workarounds.
